title: Job, a Righteous Man in the Land of Uz
image_prompt: Biblical historical realism in the ancient land of Uz, a rugged region of hills, grazing land, stone dwellings, and broad pastoral fields. Job is introduced as a blameless and upright man who fears God and turns away from evil. Portray him as a dignified, mature patriarch wearing layered earth-toned wool and linen garments, with a well-kept beard and an expression of wisdom and compassion. His household is prosperous: flocks of sheep and goats, camels, oxen, donkeys, servants, tents, and family compounds spread across the landscape. In a nearby family courtyard, his seven sons and three daughters share meals together on different occasions. Job rises early to offer burnt offerings for his children, concerned that they might have sinned in their hearts. Show an altar arranged with stones, carefully prepared wood, and a rising column of smoke. Establish Job's wealth, family affection, reverence, and moral seriousness without presenting his prosperity as modern luxury. Ancient Near Eastern material culture, natural lighting, cinematic wide shot, no modern objects.

title: The Heavenly Council and the Accuser's Challenge
image_prompt: A reverent biblical vision of a heavenly council, visually distinct from the earthly scenes in Uz. Spiritual beings present themselves before the LORD, and the Accuser appears among them. Use luminous cloud, vast celestial space, subtle radiant light, and solemn composition rather than modern fantasy armor or science-fiction imagery. The LORD asks the Accuser whether he has considered Job, His faithful servant, who is upright and turns away from evil. The Accuser argues that Job fears God because he has been protected and blessed, then challenges that Job will curse God if his possessions are taken away. The vision should communicate a serious dispute about faith, integrity, and motive. Represent divine authority through overwhelming light and throne-like majesty without forcing a literal human facial depiction. The Accuser is a distinct, serious figure, not a cartoon demon. Make the connection between this unseen council and Job's peaceful earthly life clear through a subtle visual contrast.

title: Job Loses His Children and His Possessions
image_prompt: A sequence of devastating reports converging on Job's estate. One exhausted messenger reports that Sabeans seized the oxen and donkeys and killed the servants; another reports that fire from heaven burned the sheep and shepherds; another reports that Chaldean raiders took the camels and struck down their attendants. While each messenger is still speaking, another arrives with news that Job's sons and daughters were feasting in the eldest brother's house when a great wind collapsed it, killing them. Show the ruined house at a distance, broken roof beams and dust, without graphic bodies or injuries. Job receives the reports one after another, tears his mantle, shaves his head, and falls to the ground in grief and worship. His possessions are gone and his family is dead, yet he does not accuse God of wrongdoing. Emphasize the human reality of grief, the shaken servants, and Job's devastated but reverent posture. Non-graphic, sober biblical historical realism.

title: The Accuser Challenges Job's Integrity Again
image_prompt: Return to the heavenly council as a reverent vision. The LORD asks the Accuser to consider Job, who still holds fast to his integrity despite the destruction that has come upon him. The Accuser argues that a person will surrender anything to preserve his own life and proposes that Job himself be afflicted. The LORD permits the test but places a clear limit: Job's life must be preserved. Use solemn heavenly light, a majestic but restrained composition, and a clear difference between the figures and atmosphere of the spiritual council and the earthly world. This scene is about the boundaries of the test and the continuing question of whether Job's faith is sincere. No modern objects, no sensational demonic effects, and no suggestion that Job knows what is happening in the heavenly council.

title: Job's Affliction and the Arrival of His Friends
image_prompt: Outside the settlement, Job sits among ashes, covered in painful skin sores from head to foot. Keep the condition non-graphic: show his exhausted face, weary posture, and a small clay potsherd in his hand as he scrapes himself. His wife, deeply distressed by the destruction of their family and household, asks why he still holds to his integrity and tells him to curse God and die. Job rebukes the suggestion and asks whether they should receive good from God but not adversity. Three friends—Eliphaz the Temanite, Bildad the Shuhite, and Zophar the Naamathite—hear of his trouble and travel from their regions to comfort him. They see Job from a distance, barely recognize him, weep aloud, tear their mantles, and sit beside him on the ground for seven days and seven nights without speaking because his suffering is so great. Use muted earth tones, ashes, rough ground, and solemn stillness. Do not make Job's wife a caricature or show graphic illness.

title: Job Curses the Day of His Birth
image_prompt: Job finally breaks the silence and speaks from the depth of his anguish. He curses the day of his birth and the night that announced his conception, wishing that the day had vanished from the calendar and that no light had shone upon it. Portray Job seated among ashes, shoulders bowed, looking into the dark landscape as if trying to express an unanswerable sorrow. His three friends remain silent nearby. Use a symbolic transition from a faint sunrise to a heavy, moonless night sky, with the horizon darkened and the surrounding land empty. Do not depict Job as cursing God; his lament is directed at the day of his birth and the night of his conception. The visual mood is grief, sleeplessness, and despair, rendered compassionately and without romanticizing his pain.

title: Job Asks Why the Suffering Continue
image_prompt: Continue Job's lament as he asks why he did not die at birth or perish when he came from the womb. He imagines death as a place where kings, counselors, prisoners, and the exhausted rest together, free from earthly oppression and turmoil. He asks why light is given to those in misery and why life continues for those longing for relief. Show Job speaking into the stillness while the three friends listen without interrupting. Use a dim landscape with ruined stonework, a far-off tomb entrance, and faint silhouettes of resting travelers as symbolic visual elements rather than a literal depiction of the afterlife. Job's face should communicate anguish and bewilderment rather than theatrical madness. No graphic imagery, no modern symbolism, and no claim that the friends yet understand the reason for his suffering.

title: Eliphaz Begins His First Speech
image_prompt: Eliphaz the Temanite begins speaking to Job after the long silence. He acknowledges that Job has strengthened others with his words, supported the weak, and helped those who stumbled, then questions why Job himself is overwhelmed when trouble arrives. Eliphaz argues that the innocent do not perish and that those who sow trouble reap trouble. Use a medium-wide shot of Eliphaz sitting opposite Job on the ash-covered ground, speaking earnestly but with growing certainty. A dry wind moves lightly through the sparse vegetation. Behind him, a restrained visual metaphor of a farmer sowing seed and later harvesting may suggest his argument. Include the listening Bildad and Zophar in the background. The central tension is that Eliphaz interprets Job's pain through a moral system that assumes suffering reveals wrongdoing.

title: Eliphaz Recounts a Terrifying Night Vision
image_prompt: Eliphaz describes a mysterious night vision that came when deep sleep and fear had fallen upon him. In a symbolic memory scene, show Eliphaz awake on a mat in a dark tent, startled by a faint movement and an indistinct presence passing before him. He cannot identify its form; a voice questions whether a mortal can be more righteous than God or purer than the Creator. The vision emphasizes the fragility and limited knowledge of human beings. Use a faint draft lifting the edge of the tent, lamplight nearly extinguished, and a mysterious silhouette that remains indistinct. Avoid depicting the spirit as a fully defined monster or claiming the vision provides a complete explanation of Job's suffering. Return visually to Eliphaz speaking to Job, who remains wounded and unconvinced.

title: Eliphaz Urges Job to Seek God
image_prompt: Eliphaz continues his first speech, telling Job to seek God and commit his cause to Him. He describes God as One who performs great and unsearchable works, sends rain upon the earth, raises the lowly, frustrates the schemes of the crafty, and brings hope to the poor. Show Eliphaz speaking beside a rocky hillside while the landscape behind him offers visual contrasts: dry ground receiving rain, a poor family finding shelter, and an arrogant builder's plan collapsing through ordinary consequences. These should be symbolic illustrations of Eliphaz's argument, not separate literal events occurring around Job. Eliphaz believes divine justice ultimately reverses the fortunes of the wicked and the humble. His tone is consoling in intention but prescriptive in its assumptions.

title: Eliphaz Describes the Blessing of Correction
image_prompt: Eliphaz tells Job that the person corrected by God is blessed and urges him not to despise divine discipline. He describes God as wounding and healing, rescuing from trouble, protecting through famine and war, and granting peace in old age. Show Job listening in profile, visibly exhausted, while Eliphaz gestures toward the distant hills. Use subtle visual motifs of a storm passing, a damaged wall being repaired, and an elderly household resting safely to communicate Eliphaz's promised restoration. Do not show these blessings already happening to Job or imply that Job's suffering has been proven to be punishment. The prompt should preserve the distinction between Eliphaz's confident counsel and the book's broader question about suffering.

title: Job Says His Grief Is Heavier Than the Sand
image_prompt: Job answers Eliphaz, insisting that his grief and calamity are heavier than the sand of the sea. He says his words are spoken out of overwhelming anguish and compares his pain to poisoned arrows and the terror of God. He longs for an end to his suffering but admits that his strength is exhausted and he has no power to rescue himself. Show Job seated among ashes, one hand lifted toward the friends, a wide stretch of sand and dark clouds in the distance as visual metaphors for the weight of his sorrow. Keep all depictions non-graphic. The friends must not look as though they have successfully comforted him; Job is explaining why their general principles feel inadequate to his actual condition.

title: Job Accuses His Friends of Failing Him
image_prompt: Job compares his friends to seasonal streams that appear promising but disappear when travelers need water. He says they have seen his distress and are afraid, and asks whether he ever demanded that they rescue him or bribe anyone for him. His words sharpen as he asks them to look at him honestly and consider whether his speech is unjust. Show a dry wadi cutting through the landscape, cracked earth, and a distant caravan searching for water, then return to Job facing the three friends. Eliphaz appears unsettled, Bildad watches carefully, and Zophar remains guarded. The scene emphasizes broken expectations of friendship, Job's desire to be heard, and the growing strain in the conversation.

title: Job Compares Life to Labor and a Breath
image_prompt: Job describes human life as hard service, like the days of a hired laborer who waits for shade and longs for the end of his work. He compares his nights to long hours of tossing and turning, and says his life passes more quickly than a weaver's shuttle. Show a symbolic triptych: a laborer waiting in the heat, a sleepless sufferer on a rough bed, and a weaver moving a shuttle rapidly across a loom. Job sits in the foreground, weak and restless, while his friends listen. The imagery should make clear that Job sees life as painfully brief and filled with uncertainty. Keep the ancient household setting, fabric textures, oil lamps, and natural light historically grounded.

title: Job Speaks Directly to God
image_prompt: Job turns from arguing with his friends to addressing God directly. He refuses to restrain his mouth and asks why God watches him so closely, why he is made a target, and why his suffering is not lifted. He says that if he has sinned, he does not understand why he has become such a burden, and asks why God does not pardon his transgression. Show Job looking upward into a clouded sky from the ash heap, his hands open in raw questioning rather than triumph. His expression contains pain, confusion, and a continuing desire for an answer. Do not show God visibly striking or speaking to him in this scene. The dramatic focus is the honest lament of a suffering man who still addresses God.

title: Bildad Appeals to the Wisdom of the Ancestors
image_prompt: Bildad the Shuhite begins his first speech, telling Job to ask former generations and consider what their ancestors learned. He insists that God does not pervert justice and suggests that Job's children suffered because of their transgression. He urges Job to seek God and promises that if Job is pure and upright, his future will become great. Show Bildad holding a small scroll or gesturing toward elder figures in the distance, representing inherited wisdom. Job reacts with restrained pain when his children are mentioned, while Eliphaz looks solemn and Zophar remains silent. The visual should expose the harshness of Bildad's certainty without adding an unrecorded verbal exchange.

title: Bildad's Images of Reeds and the Spider's Web
image_prompt: Bildad uses comparisons from nature: a papyrus plant cannot flourish without water, the godless person's hope is fragile, and reliance on a false foundation is like leaning on a spider's web. He also describes the flourishing of the righteous and the disappearance of the wicked. Show a papyrus plant at the edge of a shrinking pool, a delicate spiderweb on dry stone, and a green plant growing beside a sound wall. Treat these images as symbolic illustrations of Bildad's speech, not as evidence that Job is wicked. In the foreground Bildad speaks confidently, while Job's silent posture contrasts with the sweeping generalizations. The scene should communicate that traditional wisdom may contain insight yet become cruel when applied without understanding.

title: Job Acknowledges God's Unmatched Power
image_prompt: Job responds that he knows a mortal cannot easily be justified before God. He describes God's mastery over mountains, the earth, the heavens, the stars, and the sea, including constellations known as the Bear, Orion, the Pleiades, and the chambers of the south. Show Job beneath a vast night sky with recognizable star patterns, towering mountain silhouettes, and a distant sea under heavy wind. The celestial scale makes human strength seem very small. Job also describes God as acting beyond human control, and he asks who can challenge Him successfully. Keep this as poetic visual imagery rooted in Job's speech, not an astronomical chart claiming modern scientific precision.

title: Job Longs for a Mediator
image_prompt: Job explains that he would not know how to answer God, even if he could present his case, because God is powerful beyond comparison and Job feels unable to obtain a hearing. He says there is no impartial arbiter between them who can lay a hand on both. Show Job standing at the foot of an immense stone hall or beneath a towering cliff as a symbolic image of the distance he feels between himself and divine majesty. Between Job and the distant light, leave an empty space where the desired mediator is absent. His words continue into questions about why the innocent sometimes suffer and why the wicked appear to prosper. Do not depict the mediator as an actual character in this passage; the empty space is symbolic of Job's longing.

title: Job Feels Unable to Defend His Cause
image_prompt: Job compares his days to swift runners, reed boats, and an eagle swooping upon prey. He says that even if he washed himself clean, he still fears being plunged into distress again, and that God does not appear to him as an equal human adversary would. Show a montage of a runner crossing a dusty track, a light papyrus boat moving fast along a river, and an eagle descending over a rocky valley. Return to Job sitting on the ground, speaking with increasing frustration because he feels there is no neutral judge to hear him. Preserve the passage's emotional complexity: Job acknowledges God's greatness yet cannot reconcile that greatness with his own experience of suffering.

title: Job Asks Why God Formed Him Only to Afflict Him
image_prompt: Job continues his lament and asks God not to condemn him without allowing him to understand his charge. He asks whether God delights in oppressing him and describes his own formation as carefully molded like clay, woven together in the womb, and surrounded with life and favor. Show Job with a small lump of clay in his hand as a symbolic object, while a potter works clay on a low surface in a separate vignette. The image of careful formation should be reverent and metaphorical, not a literal medical depiction of pregnancy. Job's expression should hold the contradiction at the heart of his speech: he remembers receiving life and care from God, yet now feels overwhelmed by suffering.

title: Job Describes the Darkness of His Distress
image_prompt: Job says he fears that God is watching for his wrongdoing and will not regard him as innocent, while he also feels hunted and exposed. He asks why he was brought into life only to endure such pain, and he longs for a little comfort before entering a land of darkness and deep shadow. Show him seated beside a cave-like opening in a rocky hillside as dusk approaches; the darkness should represent grief and uncertainty, not a literal map of the afterlife. The friends remain present but cannot resolve his questions. Use cool twilight, rough stone, and subdued skin tones without graphic illness.

title: Zophar Rebukes Job's Words
image_prompt: Zophar the Naamathite begins speaking sharply. He accuses Job of excessive speech and suggests that Job's claims of innocence are presumptuous. Zophar argues that God's wisdom is deeper than human understanding and says that if God disclosed wisdom fully, Job would realize how much his guilt exceeds his suffering. Show Zophar leaning forward with a severe expression, one hand lifted in reprimand. Job looks toward him with pain and disbelief. Behind Zophar, use the image of a deep well and a distant mountain range as metaphors for hidden wisdom and human limitation, not as proof of Zophar's accusation. The visual should make clear that Zophar assumes guilt without evidence.

title: Zophar Promises Security If Job Repents
image_prompt: Zophar tells Job to prepare his heart, stretch out his hands to God, put away wrongdoing, and stop allowing injustice to dwell in his tents. He promises that then Job's face will be lifted without shame, his misery will be forgotten, and his future will shine like the morning. Show Zophar gesturing toward a sunrise beyond the hills and a restored household as symbolic images of the future he promises. Keep these images visually separate from the actual present, where Job remains afflicted. Zophar's closing warning contrasts the hope he offers with the fate he expects for the wicked. Do not portray Job as having accepted the accusation.

title: Job Challenges His Friends' Assumed Wisdom
image_prompt: Job answers with irony, telling his friends they are the only wise people and that wisdom will die with them. He declares that he too has understanding and is not inferior to them. Job, now an object of ridicule despite having called upon God, feels despised by those who are at ease. He points to how thieves and those who provoke God may live securely. Show the three friends seated together and Job facing them, with a prosperous tent in the far background contrasted against Job's ashes. Include nearby natural details—a tent-dweller, shepherds, and wild animals—to support Job's coming argument that creation itself teaches about God's sovereignty.

title: God's Power over Nations and the Natural World
image_prompt: Job describes wisdom and might as belonging to God, who tears down what cannot be rebuilt, shuts a person in, withholds waters, sends them out, and overturns the plans of powerful people. The passage then describes God's control over counselors, judges, kings, priests, trusted leaders, and nations. Show a symbolic panorama: a stone tower being dismantled, a river channel drying then flooding, a ruler's council interrupted, and a torchlit procession of captives moving across a rocky landscape. These are poetic illustrations of Job's argument about divine sovereignty, not one literal sequence happening to Job's own country. Use ancient Near Eastern visual language, no modern government buildings or equipment.

title: Job Demands to Speak His Case
image_prompt: Job tells his friends that he has seen and understood the things they are describing and is not inferior to them. He wants to speak directly to the Almighty and argue his case. He accuses the friends of speaking falsely for God and acting as unreliable physicians who offer no real relief. Show Job raising one hand to interrupt the friends' debate, while the three men exchange uncomfortable looks. Arrange an unused scroll and writing stylus nearby to suggest that Job wants a proper hearing. His wounds and exhaustion remain visible but non-graphic. The scene centers on his demand for honesty rather than polished religious explanations.

title: Job Risks Everything to Present His Case
image_prompt: Job asks the friends to remain silent so he can speak, even if it endangers him. He declares that though God might slay him, he will still hope in Him, and he wants to present his ways before God's face. Job asks God to reveal his offenses and wonders why he is treated as an enemy. Show Job straightening himself despite weakness, speaking toward the heavens while his friends fall quiet. A broken leaf carried by the wind and a fragile garment eaten by decay may symbolize his sense of being transient and worn down. Do not portray this as a victorious declaration that all fear has vanished; it combines faith, risk, and desperate uncertainty.

title: Job Reflects on the Brevity of Human Life
image_prompt: Job describes human beings as born of woman, living only a short time and filled with trouble, like a flower that blooms and fades or a shadow that does not remain. He wonders why God watches such a fragile creature so closely. Job contrasts a felled tree that may sprout again with a human being who appears to lie down and not rise. Show a fading wildflower beside a cut tree stump from which a small shoot has begun to grow. Job sits in the foreground beside dry stones, contemplating the brevity of life. The scene is reflective and poetic, without claiming the tree image provides a literal answer about resurrection.

title: Job Longs for Renewal and Relief
image_prompt: Job wonders whether a person who dies can live again, and imagines being hidden in the grave until God's anger passes and then being called back by God. The hope is tentative, expressed as a question and longing rather than a fully explained doctrine. Job asks God to remember him, but returns to the reality that mountains erode, stones wear away, waters undermine soil, and human hopes seem to fade. Show Job gazing toward a rocky hillside where rain has slowly worn channels into stone, with a cave entrance in the distance. Use restrained symbolism to balance hope and grief; do not depict a resurrection event occurring in Job's present.

title: Eliphaz Accuses Job of Undermining Wisdom
image_prompt: Eliphaz begins his second speech and accuses Job of speaking with empty knowledge and allowing his own mouth to condemn him. He argues that Job's words show irreverence and asks whether any mortal can be pure before God. Show Eliphaz sitting upright, voice stern, while Job listens with a guarded expression. The friends' camp now feels less like a place of comfort and more like a formal argument. Use a scroll, a closed satchel, and the harsh light of midday to heighten the sense of scrutiny. The scene must represent Eliphaz's accusations rather than confirm that Job has committed the sins alleged.

title: Eliphaz Describes the Wicked Person's Fate
image_prompt: Eliphaz appeals to what wise people have taught and paints a grim picture of the wicked person: inner torment, fear, uncertainty, and eventual ruin. He uses images of darkness, distress, and a flame that consumes what has no lasting foundation. Show a darkened landscape around a proud but isolated man whose storehouse is emptying and whose path leads into a shadowed ravine. Keep the images allegorical to Eliphaz's speech, not a literal portrait of Job's future. The final visual should contrast Eliphaz's certainty with Job's unresolved suffering, highlighting how the speech assumes that anguish must arise from wickedness.

title: Job Calls His Friends Miserable Comforters
image_prompt: Job replies that he has heard many speeches like theirs and that they are miserable comforters. He says they could strengthen him if their positions were reversed, but instead they pile words upon his anguish. Job also describes his suffering through powerful poetic images: his body is worn, his face is red from weeping, and he feels surrounded and attacked. Show Job seated upright, addressing the friends with controlled intensity, while Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar appear defensive. Use cracked ground and the silhouette of a storm-struck tree as metaphors. Keep the bodily condition non-graphic, and preserve the difference between Job's metaphorical description and a literal human attacker.

title: Job's Witness Is in Heaven
image_prompt: Job says he has sewn sackcloth over his skin and that his strength is gone, yet he believes his witness is in heaven and his record is on high. He calls for an advocate or witness who could plead on behalf of a person before God. Show Job wearing coarse sackcloth, eyes wet from tears, looking into the night sky where a small clear opening appears among clouds. Keep the heavenly witness unembodied, represented by the open sky and quiet light, because no visible individual is specified. The friends sit in shadow, unable to respond with meaningful comfort. The scene should convey Job's need for vindication and an impartial witness.

title: Job's Spirit Is Broken but His Integrity Remains
image_prompt: Job describes his spirit as broken, his days as short, and the grave as awaiting him. He feels surrounded by mockery, yet asks God to provide a pledge or guarantee and says his friends cannot understand his condition. He insists that the righteous will continue on their way and that the one with clean hands will grow stronger. Show Job leaning against a rough stone, an empty seat beside him, and the friends in a distant group. A narrow path climbing through rough terrain can symbolize the determination of the righteous. Keep Job's grief serious and empathetic; do not turn the scene into despair as spectacle.

title: Job Sees Little Hope in His Friends' Advice
image_prompt: Job invites the friends to return and try again, but says he cannot find a wise person among them. His days have passed, his plans are shattered, and those around him try to make night into day and darkness into light. He asks whether his hope can be found in the grave. Show a gathering in fading lamplight, with a dark sky beyond the tent opening and Job staring at a blank stretch of earth. The scene should visualize his uncertainty through the boundary between the lit interior and the dark outside. Do not depict death graphically or imply that Job has received a final answer.

title: Bildad Describes the Traps of the Wicked
image_prompt: Bildad begins his second speech, rebuking Job for refusing to listen and asking why the friends should be considered like beasts or fools. He then describes the light of the wicked being extinguished, their steps constrained, and traps set in their path. Show Bildad speaking from a rocky rise, with symbolic images of an oil lamp going dark, a path blocked by thorn bushes, and a hidden snare on a narrow trail. Keep these images illustrative of his general argument and not literal events around Job. The atmosphere is austere and confrontational, with Job silent in the foreground.

title: Bildad Portrays the Wicked Person as Forgotten
image_prompt: Bildad continues with images of terror, sickness, loss of family, and a name disappearing from the land. He portrays the wicked person as uprooted from his tent and forgotten by those who pass by. Show an abandoned tent, an extinguished lamp, a neglected hearth, and a path overgrown with weeds. These are poetic illustrations of Bildad's description of the wicked person's end, not proof that Job deserves such a fate. Job's ruined household may appear far behind, but avoid equating his innocent children with the wickedness described. The visual should emphasize the danger of Bildad treating a universal proverb as a definitive verdict on Job.

title: Job Says His Friends Have Wounded Him
image_prompt: Job answers that his friends have crushed him with words and asks how long they will torment him. He insists that if he has truly erred, his error remains his own; he feels that God has surrounded his path and removed his honor. Through poetic visual imagery, show Job standing before a rough earthen wall that seems to close off the road, a torn mantle hanging from his shoulders, and the remains of his former household far behind. The visual barrier is metaphorical, not a literal divine prison. His friends look stern and unconvinced. Maintain Job's dignity amid humiliation and do not imply the friends have proved their accusation.

title: Job Feels Abandoned by Everyone
image_prompt: Job laments that his relatives, acquaintances, household members, and former companions have withdrawn from him. Even those closest to him recoil, and children mock him. He asks his friends to have pity because the hand of God has touched him. Show Job at the edge of an empty courtyard, a doorway closed behind him, and a few distant figures turning away rather than approaching. The atmosphere should convey isolation without suggesting that all relationships are permanently beyond repair. Keep the friends in view so his appeal for compassion feels directed at real people who have the opportunity to respond differently.

title: Job Declares That His Redeemer Lives
image_prompt: Job longs for his words to be written with an iron pen and lead in rock so they will endure. He declares that his Redeemer lives and that ultimately he will stand upon the earth; he hopes to see God for himself, not merely hear of Him. Render this as a solemn, hopeful vision: Job beside a rock face bearing ancient carved characters, looking toward a distant ridge illuminated by dawn. The light should suggest the endurance of his testimony and longing for vindication without depicting a literal appearance of the Redeemer or claiming all interpretive questions are settled. The final part of the speech warns the friends to fear judgment themselves. Preserve the complexity of Job's conviction, grief, and hope.

title: Zophar's Second Speech Begins
image_prompt: Zophar responds quickly, saying that his troubled thoughts compel him to answer. He describes the apparent joy of the wicked as short-lived and compares their prosperity to something that disappears. He claims that even if the wicked person rises high, he will perish and be forgotten. Show Zophar speaking with rigid conviction, while Job sits silently. A tall building of mudbrick that crumbles in the wind can symbolize temporary success, but keep the imagery separate from Job's actual ruined household. The prompt should communicate that Zophar is advancing a general claim about wickedness, not establishing Job's guilt.

title: Zophar Describes the Bitter End of Wickedness
image_prompt: Zophar says that wrongdoing may taste sweet for a moment but turns bitter, and that wealth gained by injustice cannot provide lasting security. He describes terror and divine judgment overtaking the wicked. Show a symbolic banquet table with a cup left untouched, precious goods spilling from a torn storage sack, and a storm breaking over a wealthy household. The imagery must remain clearly metaphorical to Zophar's argument rather than depicting a specific future event in Job's story. Use ancient ceramics, woven cloth, oil lamps, and stone architecture; no graphic punishment.

title: Job Challenges the Idea That the Wicked Always Suffer
image_prompt: Job asks his friends to listen carefully and then be free to mock him if they choose. He says the prosperity of the wicked astonishes him: some live to old age, see their children established, enjoy secure homes, and spend their days in apparent peace. They sometimes reject God openly, yet seem to prosper. Show a split composition contrasting a comfortable household with Job seated among ashes. Do not label the prosperous household as a specific historical family; it illustrates Job's observation that worldly outcomes do not always follow the simple rule his friends propose.

title: Job Refutes His Friends' Simplistic Verdict
image_prompt: Job asks how often the wicked person's lamp truly goes out or disaster overtakes him, challenging Bildad's and Zophar's descriptions. He notes that some people die in strength and comfort while others die in bitterness, and both lie together in the dust. He argues that travelers can confirm the difference between outward prosperity and inner character, and asks how the friends can comfort him with empty words. Show a roadside conversation among travelers, a prosperous tent and a poor tent in the distance, and a quiet burial ground beyond both. Use respectful, non-graphic imagery. The panel should convey Job's insistence that real life is more complicated than his friends' moral formula.

title: Eliphaz Accuses Job of Specific Injustices
image_prompt: Eliphaz begins his third speech and goes beyond general moral principles to make direct accusations against Job. He alleges that Job has taken pledges from the poor without cause, withheld water and bread from the needy, and mistreated widows and orphans. These allegations are spoken by Eliphaz and are not established as facts by the narrative. Show Eliphaz gesturing emphatically toward Job while symbolic figures of a thirsty traveler, a poor household, and a widow stand at the edge of the composition. Keep the figures as illustrations of the accusations, not flashbacks confirming Job committed them. Job listens with hurt and disbelief.

title: Eliphaz Calls Job to Repent and Promises Restoration
image_prompt: Eliphaz says God is exalted above the heavens and sees human wrongdoing, then describes the fate of those who reject Him. He calls Job to agree with God, receive instruction, and return to the Almighty, promising that Job's path will be restored and that he will help others escape trouble. Show Eliphaz speaking against a vast sky and pointing toward a road leading to a distant settlement. Use an image of a damaged wall being repaired to illustrate restoration, but keep Job's actual condition unchanged. Make clear that Eliphaz's invitation rests on his unproven assumption that Job is guilty.

title: Job Searches for God to Present His Case
image_prompt: Job replies that his complaint remains bitter and that his suffering seems heavier than his groaning. He longs to find God's dwelling and present his case, confident that he could explain his cause if he could reach the divine court. Yet when he looks ahead, behind, to the left, and to the right, he cannot perceive God. Show Job traversing a rocky plateau in search of a path, with empty horizons stretching in every direction. His expression is determined but sorrowful. Do not show God hiding behind a literal mountain; the landscape represents Job's inability to find the audience he longs for.

title: Job Trusts That God Knows His Way
image_prompt: Job says that God knows the way he takes and that, when he has been tested, he hopes to emerge like refined gold. Job declares that he has kept to God's path and treasured His words, yet he is terrified by God's unchanging purpose and the darkness that surrounds him. Show Job following a narrow track through rugged ground, with a small goldsmith's furnace far away as a symbolic image of testing and refinement. The path is clear beneath his feet but disappears into distant shadow, communicating a mixture of conviction and fear. Do not depict the furnace as a literal test being performed upon Job.

title: Job Describes Injustice in the World
image_prompt: Job asks why times of judgment seem hidden and describes the suffering of vulnerable people. He speaks of boundaries moved by the powerful, flocks stolen, orphans deprived, widows left without protection, the poor pushed from roads, and laborers and the needy forced to hide. He also describes people who work in darkness to steal or do harm. Show a carefully composed social panorama of an ancient village: a boundary marker being shifted, a poor family searching for shelter, laborers carrying burdens, and a widow seeking help at a gate. These are examples Job raises about injustice, not accusations against named individuals in the scene. Keep the portrayal sober, historically grounded, and humane.

title: Job Questions How Quickly the Wicked Can Disappear
image_prompt: Job discusses the fate of wrongdoers, using images of swift water, drought, and the grave. He says that some are swiftly removed while others seem to flourish for a time, and challenges anyone who can prove his words false. Show a rushing stream passing through a rocky channel, a parched field, and travelers walking past abandoned dwellings. Use these images to convey Job's argument that human experience does not follow a simple, immediate pattern of punishment and reward. Do not present the scene as a final answer to the problem of injustice.

title: Bildad Speaks of God's Majesty and Human Smallness
image_prompt: Bildad gives a brief third speech, proclaiming God's dominion, peace in the heights, and the countless heavenly hosts. He asks how a mortal can be righteous before God and compares human beings to worms in their smallness. Show Bildad under a vast night sky filled with stars, with tiny human figures near the base of a massive rocky mountain. The scale should express human frailty before divine greatness, without dehumanizing Job or suggesting he deserves his affliction. Job watches silently as the conversation nears its end.

title: Job Replies with a Vision of God's Power
image_prompt: Job answers Bildad with pointed irony, asking how he has helped the powerless or enlightened the ignorant. He then describes God's power over the realm of the dead, the waters, the heavens, the earth, clouds, sea, and the fleeing serpent. Show a majestic symbolic panorama: the sea contained between rocky shores, clouds stretched across a vast sky, the horizon trembling under a storm, and the distant outline of a great serpent-like sea creature as poetic imagery. Job's friends remain small figures in the foreground. The final impression is that these are only the edges of God's ways and that His full power exceeds human understanding. Do not depict the cosmic images as modern scientific illustrations.

title: Job Maintains His Integrity
image_prompt: Job continues his discourse and swears by the living God, who has taken away his right and made his soul bitter, that he will not speak wickedness or deceit. He refuses to admit guilt simply to satisfy his friends and says he will hold fast to his righteousness as long as he lives. Show Job standing with difficulty but with a steady gaze, his friends arranged before him. The ruined landscape and his weakened condition remain visible, but his posture conveys moral resolve. The scene should show Job defending the integrity he knows in himself, not proclaiming that he is equal to God.

title: Job Describes the Portion of the Wicked
image_prompt: Job speaks of the fate that may come upon a wicked person: descendants cut off, wealth unable to protect its owner, garments and possessions taken by others, and a household vulnerable to disaster. The passage uses severe poetic descriptions to depict the instability of unjust prosperity. Show a large tent with valuables being carried away, family records scattered in the wind, and a storm approaching a settlement. Keep the scene symbolic and do not tie these events to a specific unnamed family. It should be clear that Job is speaking about the wicked in general while continuing to defend his own integrity.

title: Humans Search Deeply for Hidden Treasures
image_prompt: A poetic montage illustrates humanity's skill in mining precious metals. Miners enter shafts cut into rock, suspend lamps from beams, chip ore from dark walls, and carry stone upward in baskets. Silver has its source, gold is refined, iron comes from the earth, and copper is smelted. The miners turn darkness into light and reach places unseen by birds and beasts. Show rugged ancient mining tools, stone passages, rope supports, oil lamps, and the glow of a small furnace. The scene emphasizes human ingenuity, effort, and the ability to discover hidden material wealth, preparing for the chapter's deeper question about where true wisdom can be found.

title: Where Can Wisdom Be Found?
image_prompt: Job asks where wisdom can be found and where understanding dwells. He declares that it cannot be purchased with gold, silver, precious stones, or the treasures of the sea. No creature knows its full place, and even destruction and death have only heard of it. Show gold and gemstones laid on one side of a dark stone table while an empty seat and a scroll occupy the other; beyond them are the sea, mountains, and deep earth. The closing truth is represented simply and reverently: the fear of the Lord is wisdom, and turning away from evil is understanding. Light falls upon a person standing humbly before the Creator's vast world, without literalizing wisdom as a physical commodity.

title: Job Remembers His Former Honor
image_prompt: Job looks back to the days when he felt God's favor, his children were around him, his household prospered, and his path seemed bright. He remembers washing his steps in butter and having streams of oil near his dwelling, poetic images of abundance. He also recalls going to the city gate, where young and old honored him and leaders fell silent when he spoke. Show a dreamlike but historically grounded memory of Job in clean fine robes, walking past a prosperous estate into a crowded stone gatehouse where elders and citizens greet him with respect. Keep the present-day Job faintly visible in the composition's shadow to show that this is remembered past, not a restoration already achieved.

title: Job Remembers Defending the Vulnerable
image_prompt: Job recalls rescuing the poor who cried for help, caring for the fatherless, supporting the dying, helping widows rejoice, and serving as eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. He says he investigated unfamiliar cases and broke the power of wrongdoers. Show a series of past scenes: Job listening at the city gate to a dispute, giving support to a poor household, helping an elderly traveler, and guiding a vulnerable person through crowded streets. These are memories of Job's own account, not independent proof about every incident. His remembered influence is shown through service and justice rather than lavish display.

title: Job Describes His Humiliation
image_prompt: Job contrasts his former honor with his present disgrace. Younger men mock him, men whom he says came from impoverished and marginalized backgrounds now ridicule him, and he feels driven from society. His honor has vanished like a cloud, and terror seems to surround him. Show Job isolated near the edge of a settlement while a distant group whispers and points without turning the moment into a comic spectacle. The landscape is dusty and bleak, with abandoned pathways and harsh light. Preserve the distinction between Job's own angry description of his mockers and the worth of poor or marginalized people; do not depict poverty itself as wickedness.

title: Job Mourns His Unanswered Cry
image_prompt: Job describes sleepless nights, continuing pain, and his feeling that God has turned toward him as an adversary. He cries for help but perceives no answer, and his former music has become mourning. Show Job alone after sunset, seated beside a cold hearth, his hand against his chest and his mantle hanging loosely. A forgotten musical instrument rests nearby, and the wind moves dust through an open doorway. The mood is compassionate and sober, with no graphic illness or sensational imagery. This scene ends Job's long reflection on how far his present condition differs from his former life.

title: Job Lists His Moral Commitments
image_prompt: Job gives a formal defense of his conduct. He says he made a covenant with his eyes, rejected deceit and adultery, acted justly toward servants, and remembers that both he and his servants were formed by the same Creator. Show Job seated before the three friends as though giving testimony in a court, one hand resting on his heart and the other open toward them. In subtle background vignettes, show a household managed fairly, servants treated with dignity, and a private boundary respected. These illustrations represent the virtues Job claims for himself, not a modern courtroom or written legal affidavit.

title: Job Swears He Has Not Exploited Others
image_prompt: Job continues his oath of integrity, denying that he withheld food from the poor, failed to clothe the needy, trusted in gold, worshipped the sun or moon, rejoiced over an enemy's downfall, concealed wrongdoing, or let injustice spoil his land. He calls for the earth to reveal whether it has suffered under his actions and asks that his case be heard. Show a broad tableau of grain offered to a poor household, clothing given to someone in need, Job looking away from treasured metals, and farmers tending land. In the closing image, Job sits alone with his testimony exhausted, as though he has set down his final defense. The visual does not declare the debate resolved.

title: Elihu Steps Forward
image_prompt: Job's three friends stop answering because he maintains his innocence. Elihu son of Barachel the Buzite, from the family of Ram, becomes angry both with Job for justifying himself rather than God and with the friends for failing to answer Job adequately. Elihu has waited because he is younger, respecting the older men's age, but now speaks because he believes wisdom does not come only with years. Show Elihu standing a short distance from the seated group, young compared with the three older companions, his expression intense but controlled. The composition should clearly introduce him as a new speaker who has observed the debate and now wishes to contribute.

title: Elihu Explains Why He Has Waited to Speak
image_prompt: Elihu says he listened carefully and examined the arguments, but none of Job's friends convincingly answered Job's case. He does not want to copy their arguments or merely repeat accusations. His words, he says, are like pressure building inside him, and he must speak. Show Elihu addressing Job and the older men, with the surrounding group attentive and tense. Use a symbolic image of a wineskin stretched full or a sealed vessel under pressure beside the speaker, while ensuring it reads as a metaphor. Avoid modern glassware or an exaggerated literal burst of energy.

title: Elihu Claims to Speak Honestly
image_prompt: Elihu addresses Job directly and says he speaks sincerely, having been formed by the breath of the Almighty. He says he is a fellow human being made from clay and need not inspire terror as God does. Elihu then quotes Job's claim that God has found grounds against him and treats him as an enemy, binding his feet and watching his paths. Show Elihu standing at Job's eye level rather than towering over him, emphasizing his claim to be a fellow human. Job listens closely, with the other friends behind them. The visual should distinguish Elihu's summary of Job's complaint from an objective claim that God has literally chained Job.

title: Elihu Says God May Speak through Suffering
image_prompt: Elihu argues that God is greater than human beings and may speak in dreams, visions, correction, or through painful experiences, in order to turn a person from destructive ways and preserve life. He describes a sufferer whose body is weakened and whose strength declines. Show a symbolic sequence: a sleeper receiving a dream under a woven blanket, a person pausing at a dangerous road, and an ill man being watched over by attendants. These are illustrations of Elihu's theological interpretation, not proof that Job's affliction has this exact cause. Keep illness non-graphic and the atmosphere thoughtful rather than accusatory.

title: Elihu Describes a Messenger of Restoration
image_prompt: Elihu describes a possible messenger or mediator who can show a person what is right, leading to mercy, restored health, renewed youth, and confession of wrong. The passage presents this as a possible path through which God may rescue a person from the pit. Show a compassionate messenger standing beside a sick man, a family preparing a clean bed, and morning light entering a modest room. Keep the scene symbolic and do not identify the messenger with a specific figure that the text does not name. Elihu closes by inviting Job to answer or remain silent and learn. Job is present, listening, not yet publicly vindicated.

title: Elihu Defends God's Justice
image_prompt: Elihu turns to the other listeners and calls for discernment. He objects to Job's words that God has denied him justice and argues that God does no wickedness or injustice. He emphasizes that God repays according to a person's conduct and gives life and breath to all living creatures. Show Elihu beside a group of attentive elders, using a balance scale and the movement of breath in cold morning air as visual symbols of justice and life. Job remains part of the scene but does not endorse Elihu's argument. The image should present Elihu's conviction rather than settle the debate.

title: Elihu Says No One Can Hide from God's Judgment
image_prompt: Elihu asks his listeners to consider whether anyone who hates justice could govern, and declares that God shows no partiality to princes or the rich. He sees all human ways and can bring down rulers or expose injustice, even in darkness. Show a royal official and a poor worker standing on equal ground before a symbolic set of balanced scales, with sunlight illuminating a hidden corner of a stone hall. This is a visual illustration of Elihu's claim that divine judgment cannot be manipulated by status. Do not depict an actual king being condemned in Job's narrative.

title: Elihu Criticizes Job's Response
image_prompt: Elihu says that people should acknowledge correction and asks whether Job's words should be tested because he has spoken without full knowledge. He accuses Job of adding rebellion to his suffering and speaking against God. Show Elihu speaking with stern certainty, while Job's face reflects fatigue and disagreement. The friends remain silent and watch the exchange. Keep the camera close enough to communicate emotional tension without creating a literal courtroom with an invented judge. This panel should show Elihu's critique as his own viewpoint, not as the final judgment of the book.

title: Elihu Asks Whether Human Righteousness Can Benefit God
image_prompt: Elihu questions Job's suggestion that righteousness brings no benefit or that Job's innocence should obligate God to reward him. Elihu argues that human wrongdoing or righteousness affects other people more directly than it changes God's essential greatness. Show a person working in a community—one figure harming another and a second helping a neighbor—beneath a vast sky. The image should illustrate the difference between human consequences and God's sovereignty. Keep Job and Elihu in the foreground as the argument unfolds.

title: Elihu Says Cries for Help May Lack Understanding
image_prompt: Elihu describes people crying out under oppression yet failing to seek the Maker who gives songs in the night and teaches more than the beasts and birds. He argues that a cry may go unanswered when it is not offered with understanding, then accuses Job of speaking without knowledge. Show distressed people calling from a crowded settlement, then a quiet night scene with birds on a branch and a solitary person in prayer. This is Elihu's theological explanation and must not be shown as proof that every suffering person has prayed wrongly. Job listens, visibly unconvinced.

title: Elihu Says God Uses Power with Justice
image_prompt: Elihu continues, claiming that God is mighty yet does not despise anyone, and that He sees the righteous and the wicked. He says God may correct rulers and the afflicted, teaching the suffering and opening their ears to instruction. Show a powerful ruler and a humble laborer under the same sky, while a teacher speaks to a person who has endured hardship. Avoid portraying suffering as automatically deserved punishment; the scene represents Elihu's interpretation. Keep the ancient environment grounded in stone, timber, woven cloth, and earth-toned garments.

title: Elihu Points to God's Majesty in the Storm
image_prompt: Elihu warns Job not to be drawn toward anger or bribes and says that human wealth cannot rescue anyone from God's judgment. He then directs attention to God's works: the raising of clouds, thunder, lightning, rain, and the way the heavens announce His power. Show Elihu and the friends near a high ridge as storm clouds gather across the landscape. Lightning flickers behind distant mountains, rain begins to cross the dry ground, and the cloud edges glow in a brief opening of light. This transition foreshadows the LORD's speech from the whirlwind without making Elihu the source of the coming divine voice.

title: Thunder and Lightning Reveal the Limits of Human Understanding
image_prompt: Elihu describes his own awe at thunder, lightning, snow, heavy rain, and wind. He says these natural forces can stop human work, send animals to shelter, and serve purposes known to God. Show cattle and wild animals seeking shelter while rain moves through a rocky valley, snow gathering on high ground, and lightning illuminating distant clouds. Elihu stands on a sheltered rise, watching the weather with reverence. The visual should feel powerful but natural, recognizing that the speech interprets the storm as an expression of divine governance. No modern weather instruments, electricity infrastructure, or scientific equipment.

title: Elihu Calls Job to Consider the Wonders of God
image_prompt: Elihu asks Job to stop and consider God's wonders: how clouds balance in the sky, why the air becomes hot, and how the heavens appear firm and spread like a polished mirror. He admits that human beings cannot instruct God or fully approach His majesty. Show Job, Elihu, and the three friends looking toward a sky filled with layered clouds and pale light. A broad reflective sheet of calm water can subtly echo Elihu's polished-mirror comparison. The atmosphere is expectant as the storm gathers and the conversation approaches a decisive turning point. Elihu's words should not visually replace the actual speech of the LORD that follows.

title: The LORD Answers Job from the Whirlwind
image_prompt: The LORD answers Job out of a whirlwind. A vast, swirling storm rises across the wilderness, its center bright with mysterious light. Job and the others turn toward it, overwhelmed by the voice that demands to know who darkens counsel with words without knowledge. The LORD asks Job where he was when the foundations of the earth were laid, who measured the earth, and who set its cornerstone while the morning stars sang and the sons of God shouted for joy. Show a poetic vision of the earth's foundations, measuring line, cornerstone, and primordial waters, not a literal modern planet-building scene. The divine presence is conveyed through the whirlwind and commanding voice, not an ordinary human figure. This is the beginning of the LORD's answer, not yet a direct explanation of Job's suffering.

title: The LORD Questions Job about the Heavens and Weather
image_prompt: The LORD asks Job about the paths of light and darkness, the storehouses of snow and hail, the way lightning is sent, and the origins of rain. The questions extend to the constellations Pleiades, Orion, Mazzaroth, and the Bear with its sons, and to the provision of food for lions and ravens. Show a sweeping cosmic panorama that moves from a dawn-lit horizon to a dark night sky filled with stars, then to snow stored in mountain crevices, hail within storm clouds, lightning across a plain, and young ravens calling for food. These are poetic visions of creation's complexity, not modern scientific diagrams. Job stands small in the foreground, hearing questions that reveal how much lies beyond human knowledge.

title: The LORD Questions Job about Wild Animals
image_prompt: The LORD asks whether Job knows when mountain goats give birth or watches the labor of hinds. The questions turn to the freedom of the wild donkey, the strength and unpredictability of the wild ox, and the limits of human control over untamed creatures. Show mountain goats on steep cliffs, a hind hidden among grasses with her young, a wild donkey moving freely through open land, and a powerful wild ox refusing a harness. Job remains beneath the great landscape, observing creatures that do not answer to him. Render the animals with naturalistic detail and respectful distance, avoiding domesticated behavior or modern fences.

title: The LORD Describes the Ostrich, Horse, and Eagle
image_prompt: The LORD asks about the ostrich, which leaves its eggs in the earth and appears careless of its young, yet runs swiftly when stirred. The speech then turns to the horse's strength, its excitement before battle, and its fearless charge; the hawk and eagle also follow their appointed ways and nest high in the cliffs. Show several distinct animal vignettes: an ostrich moving across open ground, a powerful horse with mane flowing and nostrils flared, and an eagle circling above a high rocky nest. Do not place the horse in modern tack or a modern military context. The scene emphasizes the diversity, unpredictability, and wonder of the natural world, beyond Job's control.

title: Job Acknowledges His Limited Understanding
image_prompt: The LORD asks whether the one who contends with the Almighty will correct Him and tells Job to answer. Job responds that he is insignificant and places his hand over his mouth, saying he has spoken once and will not continue arguing. The LORD then challenges Job to clothe himself with majesty and execute justice if he believes he can govern the world. Show Job kneeling before the storm, lowering his hand over his mouth, while the whirlwind remains immense. Do not portray Job as being crushed or mocked; his response is a sincere recognition of the limits of his knowledge. The scene transitions from questioning Job's words to questioning whether he can exercise the authority required to govern creation.

title: The Behemoth
image_prompt: The LORD draws Job's attention to Behemoth, described as a mighty creature that eats grass like an ox, has great strength in its loins, and powerful muscles. Its bones are like bronze and its limbs like iron; it rests among lotus plants and in marshy places, unafraid when the river surges. Show a huge, formidable animal near a riverbank, with thick limbs, a powerful tail as the text describes it, and a broad body partly shaded by reeds and trees. Keep the creature grounded in the biblical poetic description rather than assigning it a definitive modern species. Job stands at a great distance, unable to control it. No fantasy armor or exaggerated monster features.

title: The LORD Asks Whether Job Can Master Leviathan
image_prompt: The LORD asks whether Job can draw out Leviathan with a hook, bind its tongue, or make it a household servant. The creature is portrayed as terrifying and untamable, not as a simple fish caught by a fisherman. Show a vast sea creature rising in dark water near rugged cliffs, its scales and formidable jaws suggested through shadow and spray. A small fishing boat and its ropes emphasize the creature's strength, but no human is shown successfully capturing it. The composition should communicate that human power and equipment are inadequate before the creature described in the poem. Avoid graphic violence, fantasy fire-breathing unless later wording is being illustrated, or modern boats.

title: Leviathan's Terrifying Strength
image_prompt: The LORD continues describing Leviathan's armor-like scales, tight seals, proud eyes, strong teeth, and invulnerable body. Its movement churns the deep into foam, while its presence makes even the mighty recoil. The closing lines describe it as fearless and proud, king over the children of pride. Show Leviathan moving through dark, turbulent water, with scales catching the light and waves breaking around its body. Use the imagery as elevated biblical poetry rather than a zoological claim about a known species. Keep the visual powerful and solemn; do not depict sailors being torn apart or add an unrelated sea battle.

title: Job Answers the LORD in Humility
image_prompt: After hearing the LORD's speeches, Job confesses that God can do all things and that no purpose of His can be thwarted. Job acknowledges that he spoke about things he did not fully understand, things too wonderful for him. He says that formerly he had heard of God by the hearing of the ear, but now his eye sees Him; therefore he retracts his words and repents in dust and ashes. Show Job kneeling on the ground, no longer arguing, while the storm has begun to clear and gentle natural light falls across the rocks. The divine presence may be represented through the fading whirlwind and radiant cloud rather than a visible human form. The scene conveys humility and a transformed understanding without suggesting Job receives a detailed explanation of why each tragedy occurred.

title: The LORD Rebukes Job's Three Friends
image_prompt: The LORD addresses Eliphaz the Temanite, saying that he and his two friends have not spoken rightly about Him as Job has. They are instructed to take seven bulls and seven rams, go to Job, and offer a burnt offering; Job will pray for them, and the LORD will accept Job's prayer rather than deal with them according to their folly. Show Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar humbled before Job, with the animals prepared for the offering and the altar arranged from stone. Job stands as the one asked to intercede. Keep the scene solemn and restorative, without portraying the friends as caricatures or showing graphic sacrifice.

title: Job's Fortunes Are Restored
image_prompt: After Job prays for his friends, the LORD restores his fortunes and gives him twice as much as he had before. His brothers, sisters, and former acquaintances come to his home, eat with him, comfort him, and give him a piece of money and a gold ring. Show Job welcomed back into a rebuilt household, sitting at a table with relatives and neighbors in a warm but historically grounded setting. His renewed livestock fill the surrounding fields: sheep, camels, oxen, and donkeys. He has seven sons and three daughters, whose names are Jemima, Kezia, and Keren-happuch; portray the daughters with dignity and include the detail that they receive an inheritance among their brothers. The closing image shows Job living many years, seeing his descendants to four generations, and dying old and full of days. The mood is restoration and continuity, without erasing the reality of the losses he experienced.
